Executive summary

Arkhiveon is not a toy. It already behaves like a real product: authentication, billing, file uploads, campaign collaboration, character systems, image workflows, family trees, and media hooks are all present. That is the good news. The bad news is that the code discipline has not kept pace with the product ambition.

The repo shows taste, intent, and some solid technical choices: TypeScript, TanStack Router, React Hook Form, Zod, Supabase, route splitting, and a distinct visual identity. But the codebase is already slipping into the classic indie SaaS trap: platform complexity without platform rigor. Large route files, very large components, broad client persistence, weak testing, and heavy bundle chunks are the main danger signals.

If this were heading to production for a paying audience, the current state would be best described as promising but not yet production-grade. The product has a stronger aesthetic point of view than many generic RPG knowledge bases, but it is still underspecified as a business. Right now it sits awkwardly between “clean focused GM tool” and “broad worldbuilding platform” without fully winning either category.

Bottom line

Ship only after a stabilization pass. The right move is not a rewrite. It is a focused hardening cycle: split the biggest surfaces, stop mutating state during render, contain heavy features behind lazy boundaries, reduce what is persisted to local storage, expand automated tests, and sharpen the product around a clearer GM-first promise.

Audit basis

This review used the actual repository, production build output, test output, selected route and component reads, Supabase migration and edge function inspection, and a local browser pass over the landing experience. The production build succeeds, but emits chunk size warnings; the largest chunks are the main app chunk at 879.33 kB minified and the PDF chunk at 1,457.41 kB minified. The main CSS bundle is also heavy at 201.37 kB.

Automated verification is thin. The repo currently runs only 3 test files and 9 tests across a much larger application surface. The largest source files are also uncomfortably large for long-term maintainability: character-sheet-fields.tsx is 1267 lines, src/routes/sheets/$characterId.tsx is 1156, family-tree.tsx is 939, auth.tsx is 934, and character-form.tsx is 934.

For market positioning, the comparison references public official feature and pricing pages from World Anvil, Kanka, and LegendKeeper as of 2026-06-23.[1][2][3][4][5][6]

Top 10 critical issues

Issue Problem Why it matters Severity Recommended solution
Oversized route and component files Key surfaces are too large: character-sheet-fields.tsx, auth.tsx, family-tree.tsx, dashboard.tsx, character-form.tsx. Large files are slower to change, harder to test, and guarantee coupling between UI, domain logic, and side effects. 9/10 Split by domain section and interaction mode. Pull form sections, feature hooks, and route loaders into dedicated modules.
Bundle containment is weak The production build ships an 879 kB main chunk and a 1.45 MB react-pdf chunk, with warning output already complaining about chunk size. This hurts first-load experience, low-end devices, and perceived polish. It also limits future growth because every new feature starts from an already heavy base. 9/10 Lazy-load heavy features aggressively, isolate PDF, graph, crop, and board tooling behind route or intent boundaries, and define manual chunks in Vite.
State mutation during render campaign-form.tsx, character-form.tsx, spell-search-dialog.tsx, and image-library-picker-dialog.tsx use inline render-time state synchronization. This is brittle React code. It increases the risk of render loops, stale updates, and hard-to-debug transitions. 8/10 Move synchronization into useEffect, derive values instead of re-storing them, and reset dialog state through explicit lifecycle hooks.
Over-persisted client state src/lib/store.ts persists campaigns, entities, logs, image assets, Spotify state, and the Spotify token in local storage. Persisting broad app state increases stale-data risk, migration cost, and XSS blast radius. Persisting an access token in local storage is specifically bad practice. 8/10 Persist only durable non-sensitive preferences and drafts. Keep tokens in memory or a server-backed session model.
Upload accounting flaw The r2-upload function updates storage usage before the signed URL upload completes, and image-storage.ts still has deletion unfinished. This creates billing/quota drift and makes storage accounting untrustworthy, which is deadly for paid plans. 8/10 Reserve usage temporarily, confirm after successful upload, reconcile failed uploads, and implement delete accounting end-to-end.
Testing is far too thin Only 3 test files and 9 tests currently protect a product with auth, billing, uploads, collaboration, forms, and dynamic systems. You will ship regressions. The surface area is already beyond what manual QA can reliably cover. 8/10 Add route smoke tests, store slice tests, form validation tests, billing flow tests, and upload failure tests. Add at least one browser E2E path.
Product onboarding is underdeveloped The product message is stylish, but the first-run value path is still vague. New users do not get a fast “create campaign, import data, invite players, run session” flow. Retention dies when the first session setup feels like work instead of momentum. 7/10 Design a guided first-session setup, starter templates, import paths, and a visible “run tonight’s session” workflow.
Monetization is present but not yet compelling Billing exists, but the premium story is not yet strong enough versus incumbents with permissions, maps, timelines, dashboards, plugins, and community layers.[1][3][5] Charging early for a narrower product is viable only if the workflow is dramatically better. Right now the differentiation is aesthetic and partial, not decisive. 8/10 Sell speed, session execution, and collaborative secrecy controls first. Do not try to out-checklist World Anvil or Kanka feature by feature.
Loading, empty, and error states are inconsistent There are isolated good patterns, but no obvious systematic standard for async surfaces across dashboard, collections, dialogs, upload flows, and edge-function failures. Inconsistent feedback makes the product feel unreliable even when it technically works. 7/10 Introduce a shared async-state pattern library with skeletons, empty-state copy rules, retry affordances, and observable error boundaries.
SEO and discoverability ceiling This is a Vite SPA with runtime metadata, which is enough for a product shell but weak for SEO-heavy acquisition or indexable public campaign content. If content marketing or public campaign pages matter, the current stack limits discoverability and rich sharing. 6/10 Add pre-rendered marketing pages, richer metadata, OG coverage, and a clear split between app shell and public content surfaces.

Code and engineering review

Architecture

The foundation is respectable. TanStack Router, form validation with Zod, and Supabase-backed persistence are modern choices. The problem is not bad tooling. The problem is too much responsibility packed into too few files. Route files and form components have become mini-applications.

The architecture is drifting toward an all-knowing client. The Zustand store combines business data, sync state, media state, activity state, and third-party integration state. That is manageable at hobby scale. At product scale it becomes a debugging tax. It also makes ownership unclear: when a bug appears, it is no longer obvious whether it lives in route composition, component local state, store persistence, or remote sync.

State management

src/lib/store.ts persists a wide set of state slices, including campaign data, image assets, activity log, Spotify session details, and the Spotify token itself. This is convenient in the short term and dangerous in the medium term. Persisting too much state creates hidden coupling between deployments, migrations, and stale browser storage.

The repo also shows render-time “synchronization” patterns in dialogs and forms. That is a code smell, full stop. The comments claim it follows React recommendations; it does not. React can tolerate this pattern in narrow cases, but using it as a general synchronization strategy is a maintenance trap.

TypeScript

The codebase is clearly TypeScript-first, which is good, and the generated database types help. But type safety is being used more as a shield than as architecture. Strong typing does not cancel out oversized components, state bloat, or weak test coverage. It reduces one class of errors; it does not solve design debt.

Performance

The build output already tells the story. The app compiles, but the app is heavy. The react-pdf chunk alone is massive, the main chunk is large enough to deserve attention, xyflow is substantial, and the app CSS bundle is not light either. There is some code-splitting, but not enough containment around the most expensive features.

The large bundle is especially painful because this product targets a use case where people want fast recall during live sessions. GMs do not care that your code is elegant if “open the sheet” or “export the PDF” causes obvious lag. This product category rewards speed under pressure.

Testing

This is the biggest quality mismatch in the repo. Nine tests is not serious coverage for a product with auth, billing, uploads, role-based collaboration, multiple entity editors, and custom sheet logic. The app is already too complex to trust intuition-driven testing.

The good news is that you do not need to chase 100% coverage. You need a sane safety net. Route smoke tests, store slice tests, form submit tests, upload failure tests, and one browser path for signup to campaign creation would already change the risk profile materially.

Security

The back end is not reckless. Supabase migrations enable row-level security and define owner-scoped policies, which is the right baseline posture for a product like this. That is a real strength and better than many early-stage apps.

The client side is looser. Persisting spotifyToken in local storage expands exposure if an XSS bug ever lands. The Spotify PKCE verifier and state in local storage are normal enough for the auth flow, but the access token should not be treated as harmless UI state. The R2 upload flow also has a quota-accounting bug: usage is incremented before the signed upload is actually confirmed, which will create support headaches once billing matters.

Accessibility

The repo is not ignoring accessibility. There is visible use of labels, ARIA attributes, and accessible component primitives across forms and dialogs. That is better than average for an indie project.

But there is no clear automated accessibility safety net, and the UI is visually dense enough that keyboard flow, focus management, reduced-motion behavior, contrast edge cases, and screen-reader semantics need a more systematic pass. Accessibility here looks partially intentional, not operationalized.

UI and UX review

UI design

The visual identity is one of the product’s best assets. The landing experience has atmosphere and a stronger editorial feel than most bland productivity clones. The app has taste. That matters in the RPG category because people want tools that feel at least vaguely aligned with the fantasy of play, not just enterprise CRUD panels.

The weakness is consistency under scale. Once the app leaves the hero surface and enters deeper forms and entity screens, the experience feels more like a growing internal tool than a tightly governed design system. The existence of a gated /design-system route is a positive sign, but the implementation quality in product screens has not fully caught up to the aspirations declared there.

Information architecture

The entity model is strong enough to support deep campaign play: characters, NPCs, sessions, items, locations, lore, sheets, images, family trees. The problem is that the IA looks like it was built from the data model outward, not from primary user goals inward.

A GM does not wake up wanting to “manage lore entries.” A GM wants to prep tonight’s session, recap the last session, pull up an NPC quickly, share a spoiler-safe view with players, and keep continuity intact. The product needs one or two explicit primary journeys that dominate the navigation and teach the rest.

Onboarding and discoverability

The landing page sells mood and broad value. It does not yet sell a fast path to activation. A new user should reach value in under five minutes with a sample campaign, pre-made entities, or an import path. Without that, the app risks feeling like another beautiful blank notebook.

The missing piece is guided momentum. The product needs “start with a one-shot,” “import your existing notes,” “build your first session pack,” and “invite players without leaking secrets.” Those are not minor polish items. They are the difference between curiosity and adoption.

Empty and error states

There are signs of care, but the async UX is not yet industrialized. When an app has uploads, billing, media, collaborative state, and multiple remote dependencies, empty states and failure states are part of the core product. Right now they read more like component-level concerns than system behavior.

Product review

What the product is trying to be

Arkhiveon appears to be an RPG campaign operating system with a stylish, quieter tone than incumbents. That is a defensible direction. “Less noise, more campaign” is a real positioning idea. The problem is that the current product still behaves like a partial worldbuilding manager rather than a fully opinionated session cockpit.

What is missing

The core missing layer is player-facing collaboration and controlled reveal. Incumbents already emphasize private-by-default sharing, granular permissions, secrets, public URLs, dashboards, maps, timelines, family trees, plugins, and webhooks.[1][3][4][5][6] Arkhiveon currently has pieces of the stack, but not yet the product narrative that makes a GM say, “Yes, this is the one I run my table from.”

Another gap is proof of retention loops. There is not yet an obvious recurring habit loop like “post-session recap,” “player update digest,” “campaign health dashboard,” “NPC relationship drift,” or “session prep checklist generated from unresolved threads.” Those are the things that make people return weekly.

Monetization potential

Billing is present, so the mechanics exist. The premium story needs sharper value packaging. A paid tier in this space should offer one of three things: save time, deepen immersion, or unlock collaboration. The current repo hints at all three, but none of them are yet dominant enough to justify strong willingness to pay.

The best monetization path is not “more storage” and not “generic pro tier.” It is feature bundling around high-emotion jobs: GM control, spoiler-safe player sharing, immersive session surfaces, AI-assisted continuity, premium templates, and export/publishing. That is how the pricing feels like a tool, not a toll booth.

Recommended product strategy

Do not try to become a worse version of World Anvil with fewer boxes checked. World Anvil already leans into massive breadth, templates, maps, timelines, and community surfaces.[3][4] Do not try to become Kanka-lite either, because Kanka has a strong free-core, modular campaign model, dashboards, family trees, webhooks, and a very practical collaboration pitch.[5][6]

The better position is this: the fastest and best-looking GM cockpit for live campaign management. If Arkhiveon wins on speed, clarity, session rhythm, and reveal control, it can beat broader tools on workflow even without beating them on sheer feature count.

Competitive analysis

World Anvil, Kanka, and LegendKeeper are the correct comparison set. Together they define the expectation envelope for this category: deep worldbuilding structure, campaign organization, maps, timeline tooling, collaboration, controlled sharing, and premium differentiation.[1][2][3][4][5][6]

Missing features versus the field

  • Granular player visibility and spoiler-safe publishing as a first-class workflow
  • Maps, timelines, and public/private knowledge presentation
  • Dashboarding and role-specific or audience-specific views
  • Import/export flows that feel like a migration path, not a backup utility
  • Clear community or template ecosystem hooks
  • Offline-first or at least resilient low-connectivity support

Unique positioning opportunity

Arkhiveon should position itself as the product that keeps a GM in flow during active play. That means fast entity recall, session packet generation, player-safe reveal mode, consequence tracking, continuity alerts, character relationship views, and recaps that write themselves. That is a narrower promise than “all-in-one worldbuilding,” but it is far more winnable.

Top 10 quick improvements

  1. Stop calling setState during render in the dialog and form surfaces.
  2. Lazy-load react-pdf, family tree, cropper, and board-heavy flows only when the user explicitly opens them.
  3. Remove spotifyToken from persisted local storage state.
  4. Add a shared skeleton, empty state, and retry pattern for every async route.
  5. Add one “new campaign in under 3 minutes” onboarding path.
  6. Add route smoke tests for auth, dashboard, collections, billing, and image upload.
  7. Split auth.tsx into login, signup, and pricing-mode sections.
  8. Break character-form.tsx and character-sheet-fields.tsx into system-specific modules.
  9. Fix storage accounting so quota is finalized only after upload success.
  10. Define manual chunking for PDF, graph, whiteboard, and media dependencies.

Code examples

1. Replace render-time synchronization

Current dialog and form patterns reset state during render. That should move into a controlled effect.

useEffect(() => {
  if (!open) {
    setSearchQuery('');
    setLevelFilter('all');
    setSchoolFilter('all');
    setShowHomebrewForm(false);
    setSelectedSpell(null);
    resetHbForm();
    return;
  }

  setStep(isEdit ? 'form' : 'system');
  setActiveSection('identity');
  setSelectedLayoutTemplateId(character?.customTemplateId);
}, [open, isEdit, character, resetHbForm]);

2. Isolate expensive features behind lazy boundaries

react-pdf should not sit anywhere near the critical path for a user who is just browsing characters or notes.

import { lazy, Suspense } from 'react';

const CharacterSheetPdfDialog = lazy(
  () => import('@/components/character-sheet-pdf')
);

function ExportSheetButton() {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);

  return (
    <>
      <Button onClick={() => setOpen(true)}>Export PDF</Button>
      {open && (
        <Suspense fallback={<Spinner label="Loading PDF tools" />}>
          <CharacterSheetPdfDialog />
        </Suspense>
      )}
    </>
  );
}

3. Persist less state and never persist third-party access tokens

The persisted store should contain durable user data and preferences, not broadly scoped session secrets.

persist(createStore, {
  name: 'arkhiveon-storage',
  partialize: (state) => ({
    activeCampaignId: state.activeCampaignId,
    campaigns: state.campaigns,
    customTemplates: state.customTemplates,
    preferences: state.preferences
    // do not persist spotifyToken, activity log, transient upload state,
    // or large image-derived structures unless there is a hard requirement
  })
});

4. Finalize storage usage only after upload success

The signed URL flow should reserve or defer quota, then confirm after the PUT succeeds.

// server outline
const reservation = await createUploadReservation(userId, fileSize);
const signedUrl = await issueSignedUrl(reservation.key);
return { signedUrl, reservationId: reservation.id };

// client
await fetch(signedUrl, { method: 'PUT', body: file });
await supabase.functions.invoke('r2-confirm-upload', {
  body: { reservationId }
});

Overall verdict

Technical score: 58/100

UX score: 61/100

UI score: 68/100

Product score: 64/100

Scalability score: 55/100

Arkhiveon has more potential than most indie RPG tools because it already has product taste and platform ambition. But right now it is trying to carry too much weight in the client, in too few files, with too little verification. That is survivable if corrected now. It becomes expensive if allowed to harden into the product’s permanent shape.

The right next move is not feature frenzy. It is stabilize, narrow, and sharpen. Make the app feel brutally reliable for one core use case: helping a GM run and remember a campaign better than any other tool. Once that is undeniable, the broader platform ambitions become believable instead of speculative.
